en: Theravāda Vinayapiṭaka Cūḷavagga 21.
Pañcasatikakkhandhaka (The Chapter on the Five Hundred)
1. The Introduction to the Council Then the Venerable Mahākassapa addressed the bhikkhus:
“Friends, on one occasion I was traveling along the highway from Pāvā to Kusinārā together with a great saṅgha of bhikkhus, numbering about five hundred.”
Then, friends, having descended from the road, I sat down at the foot of a certain tree.
Now at that time, a certain Ājīvaka was traveling along the highway from Kusinārā toward Pāvā, carrying a mandārava flower.
I saw that Ājīvaka coming from afar, friends.
Having seen that Ājīvaka, I said to him:
“Friend, do you know our Teacher?
“Yes, friend, I know him.”
"Today the ascetic Gotama attained final Nibbāna.
It was for that reason that I took this mandārava flower.
In that regard, friends, those bhikkhus who were not yet free from passion—some of them, raising their arms, wailed; they fell down as if struck, rolled back and forth, and writhed about.
"Too soon has the Blessed One attained final Nibbāna; too soon has the Sugata attained final Nibbāna; too soon has the Eye of the World disappeared.
But those monks who were free from lust endured it mindfully and with clear comprehension, thinking:
"Conditioned phenomena are impermanent; how could this be otherwise?"
Then, friends, I said this to those bhikkhus:
“Enough, friends; do not grieve;
do not lament.”
"Surely, friend, this has already been declared by the Blessed One:
'With all that is dear and appealing, there must be change, separation, and alteration.
How, friend, could it be possible here that what is born, come to being, conditioned, and subject to disintegration should not disintegrate?"
‘This is impossible.
Now at that time, friends, an elderly renunciant named Subhadda was sitting in that assembly.
Then, friends, the elderly renunciant Subhadda said this to those bhikkhus:
“Enough, friends, do not grieve;
do not lament.
We have been well released from that Great Ascetic.”
"We were oppressed by [the rules]:
'This is permitted for you; this is not permitted for you.
But now we shall do whatever we wish, and we shall not do what we do not wish."
Come now, friends, let us recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya together.
Before the non-Dhamma shines forth and the Dhamma is suppressed;
before the non-Vinaya shines forth and the Vinaya is suppressed.
“Formerly, those who spoke what is contrary to the Dhamma were powerful, while those who spoke according to the Dhamma were weak;
formerly, those who spoke contrary to the Vinaya were powerful, while those who spoke according to the Vinaya were weak.
“In that case, Bhante, let the Elder select the monks.”
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa selected four hundred and ninety-nine Arahants.
The bhikkhus said to the Venerable Mahākassapa:
"Venerable sir, although this Venerable Ānanda is still a trainee, he is incapable of going on a wrong path through desire, hatred, delusion, or fear."
“Furthermore, he has mastered much of the Dhamma and the Vinaya in the presence of the Blessed One.
Therefore, venerable sir, let the Elder choose the Venerable Ānanda as well.
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa chose the Venerable Ānanda too.
Then it occurred to the elder bhikkhus:
"Where indeed should we recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya?
Then it occurred to the elder bhikkhus:
“Rājagaha indeed has a vast alms-resort and abundant lodgings; what if we were to spend the rains retreat at Rājagaha and recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya?
Let no other bhikkhus enter the rains retreat at Rājagaha.
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa made this known to the Saṅgha.
“Let the Sangha hear me, friends.
If it seems appropriate to the Sangha, let the Sangha authorize these five hundred bhikkhus—
to spend the rains residence at Rājagaha and recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya— and that no other bhikkhus should spend the rains residence at Rājagaha.”
This is the motion.
Let the venerable Saṅgha hear me:
these five hundred bhikkhus are being appointed.
"Let these five hundred bhikkhus dwell in Rājagaha for the rains retreat in order to recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya; no other bhikkhus should dwell in Rājagaha for the rains retreat.

To whichever venerable one it is agreeable that these five hundred bhikkhus be authorized to dwell in Rājagaha for the rains retreat in order to recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya, and that no other bhikkhus should dwell in Rājagaha for the rains retreat..."
Therefore, he who approves should remain silent; he who does not approve should speak.
These five hundred bhikkhus, authorized by the Saṅgha, shall dwell for the rains at Rājagaha and recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya; no other bhikkhus are to dwell for the rains at Rājagaha.
"It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore it is silent. Thus do I understand this.
Then the elder bhikkhus went to Rājagaha to recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya.
Then it occurred to those elder bhikkhus:
“Friends, the Blessed One has praised the repair of what is broken and dilapidated.
Come, friends, let us repair what is broken and dilapidated during the first month;
then, having assembled during the middle month, we shall recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya.”
Then the elder bhikkhus repaired the dilapidations during the first month.
Then the Venerable Ānanda thought:
"The assembly is tomorrow; it would not be fitting for me, being still a trainee, to go to the assembly."
Having spent much of the night with mindfulness directed to the body, at the time of dawn he inclined his body, thinking, "I shall lie down.
Before his head reached the pillow and before his feet were released from the ground,
in that interval his mind was liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
Then the Venerable Ānanda, having become an arahant, went to the assembly.
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa informed the Saṅgha:
"Let the Saṅgha, friends, hear me."
“If it is timely for the Saṅgha, I would question Upāli on the Vinaya.
Venerable Upāli made a formal announcement to the Saṅgha:
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me.”
“If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, I shall answer when questioned on the Vinaya by the Venerable Mahākassapa.
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa said this to the Venerable Upāli:
“Friend Upāli, where was the first offense entailing expulsion (pārājika) laid down?”
“At Vesālī, Bhante.
“Concerning whom?
“Concerning Sudinna Kalandaputta.”
“In what matter? “In the matter of sexual intercourse.
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa asked the Venerable Upāli about the matter for the first *pārājika* offense as well.
He asked about the origin, he asked about the individual, he asked about the formal rule, he asked about the subsequent rule,
he asked about the offense,
and he asked about the non-offense. "But, friend Upāli, where was the second *pārājika* laid down?"
“In Rājagaha, Bhante.
“Concerning whom?
“Concerning Dhaniya, the potter’s son.”
“In what matter? “In the taking of what is not given.
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa asked the Venerable Upāli about the matter for the second pārājika offense as well.
He asked about the origin, he asked about the individual, he asked about the formal rule, he asked about the subsequent rule,
he asked about the offense,
and he asked about the non-offense. "But, friend Upāli, where was the third *pārājika* laid down?"
“At Vesālī, Bhante.
“Concerning whom?
“Concerning a number of bhikkhus.”
“In regard to what matter?
“In regard to a human being.
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa asked the Venerable Upāli about the matter for the third pārājika offense as well.
He asked about the origin, he asked about the person, he asked about the formal promulgation, he asked about the subsequent promulgation,
he asked about the offense, and he asked about the non-offense: "But, friend Upāli, where was the fourth *pārājika* rule promulgated?"
“At Vesālī, Bhante.
“Concerning whom?
“Concerning the bhikkhus dwelling on the banks of the Vaggumudā River.”
“In regard to what matter? “In regard to a superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma).
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa asked the Venerable Upāli about the matter of the fourth *pārājika* offense as well.
He asked about the origin, he asked about the person, he asked about the formal rule, he asked about the subsequent rule, he asked about the offense,
and he asked about the non-offense. By this very method,
he questioned both sections of the Vibhaṅga.
Being questioned again and again, the Venerable Upāli answered.
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa informed the Saṅgha:
"Let the venerable Saṅgha listen to me.
“If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, I would question the Venerable Ānanda about the Dhamma.
The Venerable Ānanda informed the Saṅgha:
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me.
“If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, when asked about the Dhamma by the Venerable Mahākassapa, I shall answer.
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
“Friend Ānanda, where was the *Brahmajāla* spoken?”
“Between Rājagaha and Nāḷandā, at Rājagāraka, near Ambalaṭṭhikā, venerable sir.
“With reference to whom?
“With reference to the wanderer Suppiya and the young Brahmin Brahmadatta.”
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa asked the Venerable Ānanda about the introduction to the *Brahmajāla Sutta* and also about its personages:
"But, friend Ānanda, where was the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta* spoken?
"At Rājagaha, Bhante, in Jīvaka’s Mango Grove," he replied.
“With whom? “With Ajātasattu, the son of Vedehiputtā.
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa asked the Venerable Ānanda about the occasion for the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta*, and he also asked about the person.
By this same method, he questioned [the monks] regarding all five Nikāyas.
Each time he was questioned, the Venerable Ānanda answered.
2. The Discussion on the Minor and Lesser Training Rules (Khuddānukhuddaka-sikkhāpada-kathā).
Then the Venerable Ānanda said this to the elder bhikkhus:
“Venerable sirs, at the time of his final nibbāna, the Blessed One said to me:
‘Ānanda, if the Saṅgha so desires, after my passing away, it may abolish the minor and lesser training rules.’”
“But did you ask the Blessed One, friend Ānanda:
‘But which, Bhante, are the minor and lesser training rules?
“I did not ask the Blessed One that, Bhante.”
“But which, venerable sir, are the minor and lesser training rules?
Some elders spoke thus:
“With the exception of the four rules entailing expulsion, the remaining ones are the minor and lesser training rules.”
Some elders spoke thus:
"Excluding the four *pārājika* rules and excluding the thirteen *saṅghādisesa* rules, the remaining training precepts are minor and secondary.
Some other elders spoke thus:

“Excluding the four *pārājika* rules, excluding the thirteen *saṅghādisesa* rules, and excluding the two *aniyata* rules, the remaining ones are the minor and lesser training rules (*khuddānukhuddaka-sikkhāpada*).
Some elders spoke thus:

“Excluding the four *pārājika* rules, excluding the thirteen *saṅghādisesa* rules, excluding the two *aniyata* rules, and excluding the thirty *nissaggiya-pācittiya* rules, the remaining ones are the minor and lesser training rules.”
Some elders spoke thus: "Excluding the four *pārājika* rules, excluding the thirteen *saṅghādisesa* rules, excluding the two *aniyata* rules,
excluding the thirty *nissaggiya-pācittiya* rules, and excluding the ninety-two *pācittiya* rules, the remaining ones are the minor and lesser training rules (*khuddānukhuddaka-sikkhāpada*)."
Some elders spoke thus: “Excluding the four *pārājika* offenses, excluding the thirteen *saṅghādisesa* offenses, excluding the two *aniyata* offenses,
excluding the thirty *nissaggiya-pācittiya* offenses, excluding the ninety-two *pācittiya* offenses, [and] the four *pāṭidesanīya* offenses...”
"Excepting these, the remaining rules of training are minor and lesser matters.
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa informed the Saṅgha:
"Let the venerable Saṅgha listen to me.
Our training rules have become known among householders.
Even householders know:
"This is allowable for you, the recluses, sons of the Sakyans; this is not allowable for you."
“If we were to abolish the minor and lesser training rules, there would be those who would say:
‘The ascetic Gotama laid down the training rules for his disciples only until the time of his passing away;
as long as they had a teacher, they trained in these training rules.’”
"Since our Teacher has attained final Nibbāna, they no longer train in the rules of training.

If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha not lay down what has not been laid down, let it not abolish what has been laid down, and let it proceed by undertaking and practicing according to the rules of training as they have been laid down.
This is the motion.
"Friends, let the Saṅgha hear me.
Our training rules have become known to householders;
even householders know them."
‘This is permissible for you, recluses, sons of the Sakyans; this is not permissible for you.
If we were to abolish the minor and lesser training rules, there would be those who would say:
‘The recluse Gotama has laid down the training rules for his disciples only until the smoke [of his teaching] has vanished.’
"As long as these teachers remained, so long did they train in the training rules.
But since their teachers have attained final nibbāna, they no longer train in the training rules. [In response, the Buddha said:

"The Saṅgha does not lay down what has not been laid down, nor does it abolish what has been laid down; it proceeds by undertaking and practicing the training rules exactly as they have been laid down."

Whichever venerable one approves of not promulgating what has not been promulgated, of not abolishing what has been promulgated, and of undertaking and practicing the training rules as they have been promulgated—let him be silent.
Whoever does not approve, let him speak.
The Sangha does not promulgate what has not been promulgated, it does not abolish what has been promulgated, and it undertakes and practices the training rules as they have been promulgated.
“It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore it is silent. Thus do I hold this.
Then the elder bhikkhus said to the Venerable Ānanda:
“This is an offense of wrong-doing for you, friend Ānanda, in that you did not ask the Blessed One: ‘But which, Bhante, are the minor and lesser training rules?’”
“Confess that misdeed.
“Venerable sir, it was through lack of mindfulness that I did not ask the Blessed One, ‘But which, venerable sir, are the minor and lesser training rules?
I do not see that as a misdeed; nevertheless, out of faith in the Venerable Ones, I confess that misdeed.”
“Friend Ānanda, this too is an offense of wrong-doing for you, in that you sewed the Blessed One’s rainy-season robe after having stepped on it.
Confess that offense of wrong-doing.
“Venerable sir, it was not out of disrespect that I sewed the Blessed One’s rainy-season robe after having stepped on it.”
“I do not see that as an offense; however, out of faith in you, venerable ones, I confess that offense.
“Even this, friend Ānanda, is an offense for you: that you had the Blessed One’s body saluted first by women, so that while they were weeping, the Blessed One’s body was smeared with their tears.
Confess that offense.”
“Venerable sir, thinking, ‘May the women not have to pay their respects to the Blessed One’s body at an improper time,’ I had the women pay homage to the Blessed One’s body first.
I do not see that as a transgression; nevertheless, out of respect for the venerable ones, I confess that transgression.

“This too, friend Ānanda, is a transgression on your part, in that when the Blessed One was giving such a gross hint, when he was giving such a gross indication, you did not ask the Blessed One [to remain].”

“May the Blessed One remain for an eon! May the Sugata remain for an eon, for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans!
“Confess that misdeed.
“Venerable sir, my mind was possessed by Māra; I did not request the Blessed One [to pass away].”

“May the Blessed One remain for an eon! May the Sugata remain for an eon, for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, and for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans!
“I do not see that as a transgression; nevertheless, out of faith in the Venerable Ones, I confess that transgression.
“This too is a transgression for you, friend Ānanda, in that you made an effort for the going-forth of women in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.”
“Confess that misdeed.
“Venerable sir, this Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī is the Blessed One’s maternal aunt, his nurse, his foster-mother, the giver of milk;
when the Blessed One’s mother passed away, she suckled him at her breast. [Yet] in the teaching proclaimed by the Tathāgata, she is a woman...”
"I made an effort for the going-forth in the Dhamma and Vinaya.
I do not see that as a transgression; nevertheless, out of faith in the Venerable Ones, I confess that transgression.
Now at that time, the Venerable Purāṇa was wandering on tour in the Southern Hills together with a large Saṅgha of monks, numbering about five hundred monks.
Then the Venerable Purāṇa, after the Elder bhikkhus had chanted the Dhamma and the Vinaya,
having dwelt as long as he desired in Dakkhiṇāgiri, approached Rājagaha, Veḷuvana, the Kalandaka Feeding Ground,
and where the Elder bhikkhus were; having approached them and exchanged greetings with the Elder bhikkhus, he sat down to one side.
As the Venerable Purāṇa was sitting to one side, the elder bhikkhus said to him:
“Friend Purāṇa, the Dhamma and the Vinaya have been chanted together by the elders;
come, join in that chanting.”
“Friends, the Dhamma and the Vinaya have been well-rehearsed by the elders.
Nevertheless, I shall retain them exactly as I heard them in the presence of the Blessed One and received them from his own mouth.
3. The Discourse on the Brahma-Daṇḍa (The Censure of Brahmā)
Then the Venerable Ānanda said this to the elder bhikkhus:
“Venerable sirs, at the time of his final Nibbāna, the Blessed One said to me:
‘In that case, Ānanda, after my passing, let the Saṅgha impose the Brahma-penalty upon the bhikkhu Channa.’”
“But did you ask the Blessed One, friend Ānanda:
‘But what, Bhante, is the Brahma-punishment?
“I did indeed ask the Blessed One, Bhante.”
“But what, venerable sir, is the Brahma-punishment?
“Ānanda, whatever Channa the bhikkhu wishes, he may say.
The bhikkhus must neither speak to Channa the bhikkhu, nor exhort him, nor instruct him.”
“Therefore, friend Ānanda, you yourself should impose the Brahma-penalty upon the monk Channa.
“But how, Bhante, shall I impose the Brahma-penalty upon the monk Channa? That monk is fierce and harsh.
“In that case, friend Ānanda, go together with many monks.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the elder bhikkhus.
Together with a great community of bhikkhus, numbering about five hundred, he sailed upstream from Kosambī by boat.
Having disembarked from the boat, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree not far from King Udena’s park.
Now at that time, King Udena was enjoying himself in the park together with his harem.
The king’s harem heard:
“It is said that our teacher, the venerable Ānanda, is sitting at the foot of a certain tree not far from the park.”
Then King Udena’s harem said this to King Udena:
“It seems, Your Majesty, our teacher, the venerable Ānanda, is sitting at the foot of a certain tree not far from the park.
We wish, Your Majesty, to see the venerable Ānanda.”
“In that case, you should see the ascetic Ānanda.
Then the king Udena’s harem approached the Venerable Ānanda; having approached and paid homage to the Venerable Ānanda, they sat down to one side.
As they were seated to one side, the Venerable Ānanda instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the king Udena’s harem with a discourse on the Dhamma.

Then King Udena’s harem, having been instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by the Venerable Ānanda with a discourse on the Dhamma, presented the Venerable Ānanda with five hundred upper robes.

Then King Udena’s harem, having rejoiced and expressed their appreciation for the Venerable Ānanda’s words, rose from their seats, paid homage to the Venerable Ānanda, and keeping him to their right, approached King Udena.
King Udena saw the harem approaching from afar.
Having seen them, he said this to the women of the harem: “Did you see the ascetic Ānanda?
“We did not see the noble Ānanda, Your Majesty.”
“Have you perhaps given anything to the ascetic Ānanda?
“We have indeed, Your Majesty; we gave five hundred upper robes to the noble Ānanda.
King Udena complained, grumbled, and became indignant.
“How can it be that the ascetic Ānanda accepts so much robe-cloth?
Is the ascetic Ānanda going to engage in the trade of cloth, or is he going to open a shop for receiving goods?
Then King Udena approached the Venerable Ānanda and exchanged greetings with him.
Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, he sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, King Udena said to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Has our harem, Master Ānanda, arrived here?"
“Your harem, Great King, has indeed come here.
“But did she give anything to Master Ānanda?
“She gave me five hundred upper robes, Great King.”
“But what will the venerable Ānanda do with so much robe-cloth?
“Great King, I shall share it with those monks whose robes are worn out.
“And as for those old, worn-out robes, Master Ānanda, what will you do with them?”
“We shall make them into upper coverlets, Great King.
“But as for those old upper coverlets, Master Ānanda, how will you deal with them?
“We shall make them into mattress skins, Great King.”
“But, Master Ānanda, what will you do with those old medicinal bark-skins?
“We shall use them as floor coverings, Great King.
“But, Master Ānanda, what will you do with those old floor coverings?”
“We shall make foot-wipers out of them, Great King.
“But as for those old foot-wipers, Master Ānanda, how will you dispose of them?
“We shall make dust-removers out of them, Great King.”
“But as for those old dust-cloths, Master Ānanda, what will you do with them?
“We shall grind them up, mix them with mud, and plaster the walls, Great King.
Then King Udena thought, “All these recluses, sons of the Sakyans, act with proper reflection; they do not follow their lineage.”
He also gave five hundred other pieces of cloth to the Venerable Ānanda.
This was the first gift of robe-cloth that arose for the Venerable Ānanda, amounting to one thousand robes.
Then the Venerable Ānanda went to the Ghosita Monastery; having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Then the Venerable Channa approached the Venerable Ānanda; having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Ānanda and sat down to one side.
As the Venerable Channa was sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said this to him:
"Friend Channa, the Brahma-punishment has been pronounced against you by the Saṅgha."
“But what, venerable Ānanda, is this ‘brahma-punishment’ that has been pronounced?
“Friend Channa, you may say whatever you wish to the monks.
But you are not to be addressed by the monks, nor exhorted, nor instructed.”
“Am I not, venerable Ānanda, already ruined by this much, since I am neither to be spoken to, nor exhorted, nor instructed by the bhikkhus? Having said this, he fainted and fell right there.

Then the Venerable Channa, distressed, ashamed, and disgusted by the Brahma-punishment, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, before long attained that supreme goal for which young men of good family rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness.
Having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the culmination of the holy life, he dwelt therein.
He directly knew: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
And the Venerable Channa became one of the Arahants.
Then the Venerable Channa, having attained arahantship, approached the Venerable Ānanda and said to him:
“Venerable Ānanda, please now lift the Brahma-penalty from me.
“Friend Channa, at the very moment you realized arahantship, your Brahma-penalty was lifted.”
In this recitation of the Vinaya, there were exactly five hundred bhikkhus, neither fewer nor more.
Therefore, this recitation of the Vinaya is called the "Recitation of Five Hundred.
This is the eleventh chapter, the Chapter on the Five Hundred. In this chapter, there are twenty-three narrative bases (vatthu).
Its summary verse:
When the Perfectly Enlightened One had attained final Nibbāna,
there was an elder named Kassapa.
The protector of the true Dhamma addressed the assembly of monks on the road leading toward Pāvā.
It has been proclaimed by Subhadda:
"We shall chant the true Dhamma,
for unrighteousness is about to shine forth."
He selected four hundred and ninety-nine [monks], and Ānanda as well;
[they held] the rehearsal of the Dhamma and Vinaya.
Vasanta questioned Guha on the supreme [Vinaya], and Upāli questioned Ānanda,
the scholar of the Suttantas, on the Vinaya.
The disciples of the Victor compiled the Piṭaka in three collections through the three councils;
[they included] the various minor and lesser rules.
By acting according to the prescribed rule,
he did not ask [for permission] after stepping over [the threshold];
he caused [them] to pay homage and made no request.
The going forth of women,
the offenses of wrong-doing through faith,
the ancient [rule], and the Brahma-punishment.
The obstruction together with the lack of food;
likewise, the abundance, the weakness,
the upper blanket, and the mattress.
Carpet covers, wiping cloths,
and tools for removing dust and mud;
a thousand robes were produced.
Known as the First Bliss,
he was struck by the Brahma-punishment and attained the Four Noble Truths.
Five hundred [nuns] became masters;
therefore, it is called "The Chapter of the Five Hundred.
The Chapter on the Five Hundred is finished.
